doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Hearing the music live: being in the room
summary: They stress the importance of seeing great players in person, with Nussbaum comparing record sound to live sound for Getz and Joe Henderson.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That’s a big list. I mean I wish I’d been able to see people like Bird, Bud Powell, I mean Coltrane. Because the energy and the feeling you get from the recorded medium is phenomenal but that never approaches what it’s like to be in the room. I mean when you’re in the room with the sound it changes your life forever. I mean the first time I heard Miles Davis is was like, or the first time you, like I remember the first time I sat next to Philly Joe Jones and it was like oh man. Those things, you never forget that, and being able to have heard Bird or these cats, Bud. My God, what an amazing experience. And to get to play with them would have been an astounding treat.

What you just said about being in the room, that’s the thing right there. Not a record, not a CD, but being in the room. Like I would love to have been sitting somewhere in a room where Tatum was playing.

That would have been unbelievable. It would have been just unbelievable because that’s kind of like going back to my uncle playing the piano, there could have been nothing better than being in the room, hearing this right here. There’s no separation, no second generation or anything. Nothing like it. Which is an important thing for the educational system to realize is that to really develop great young players they need to be in the room.
They need to be in the room with the sound.
I mean I can’t stress it enough. To be in the room and hear somebody that really plays great. To be next to them. To be in the room with the sound and experience it first hand.

Yeah, that’s reality. It’s like I make the analogy a lot of times when I’m doing a clinic, I’ll say well do you just want to read the sex manual and look at the videos? Or do you want to be right in there and enjoy that.
That gets their attention I bet.

That gets their attention. But you’ve got to be there. I mean there’s nothing like being on the bandstand playing with it. But to be in the room, to be a drummer and to watch how this motion makes the sound. To feel what’s going on. To see how the horn player plays. To watch their whole physical being and to feel the sound. I mean I was deceived for many years when I used to listen to records, because whenever I used to hear Stan Getz on a record he had that soft, gentle tone. And then I would hear Joe Henderson on a record, and he had this really firm core on his sound. So I’m thinking Joe’s got this real big sound, and Stan has got this gentle sound. Then I got on the bandstand with Joe and it was a small, he’s not loud, not loud at all, but he had a very firm core to his sound.
